1.note: Ezekiel is using the term **behold** to express his surprise at what he saw. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation as modeled in the UST.
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:22.
See how you translated this word in 1:26.

The point of this comparison is that just as a **throne** has a particular shape and appearance, so did the thing that Ezekiel saw above the cherubs. Ezekiel is careful to say only that it looked like a throne. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [an object shaped and appearing like a throne]

The expression **was seen** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I saw something like the appearance of the likeness of a throne]

2.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, who was seated on the throne. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh said]
Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean coals that were on fire. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [live coals]

Ezekiel is using **to my eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “as I watched.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while I looked at him]

3.note: Ezekiel is providing background information in this verse to help readers better understand the events in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

4.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:28.
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:3.

The expression **was filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you use an active form, **the cloud** would be the subject. Alternate translation: [And the cloud filled the house]

Ezekiel is using the possessive form to describe the **brightness** that came from **the glory of Yahweh**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with the brightness that shone from the glory of Yahweh]

5.note: The expression **was heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Ezekiel does not say who heard the sound, so if you use an active form, you could use a general subject such as “people.” Alternate translation: [was loud enough for people to hear]

The point of this comparison is that just as the voice of **the Almighty when he speaks** is loud and powerful, so was **the sound of the wings of the cherubs**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and it was loud and powerful, like the voice of God Almighty when he speaks]

6.note: In this verse and the next Ezekiel is providing background information to help readers better understand the events of the story. He is now giving more details about the events that he already told us about in verse 2. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.
Here, **fire** represents the “coals of fire” from verse 2. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the expression from verse 2. Alternate translation: [coals of fire]

The term **wheelwork** describes the set of wheels that were beside the cherubs and that moved along with them. If your readers would not be familiar with this term, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the set of wheels]

The pronoun **he** refers to **the man clothed in linen**, not to Yahweh, who gave the command. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Then the man clothed in linen went, and he stood]

7.note: Ezekiel is using **sent his hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “reached out his hand.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then the cherub stretched out his hand]

The pronoun **it** in this verse refers to **the fire**, which represents the burning coals of fire. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he lifted the fire] or [and he lifted the coals of fire]

8.note: Ezekiel is providing further background information to help readers understand what happed in the previous verse. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **was seen** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you use an active form, you could indicate that Ezekiel is the one who saw it. Alternate translation: [And I saw on the cherubs]

Ezekiel is using the possessive form to describe a **form** that is characterized by having the shape of **a hand of a man**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something shaped like a human hand]

9.note: Ezekiel is using the term **behold** to express his amazement at what he saw. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and again I saw an amazing thing]

9.q: אוֹפַ֣ן אֶחָ֗ד אֵ֚צֶל הַ⁠כְּר֣וּב אֶחָ֔ד וְ⁠אוֹפַ֣ן אֶחָ֔ד אֵ֖צֶל הַ⁠כְּר֣וּב אֶחָ֑ד
9.note: Ezekiel is using **one wheel beside the one cherub, and one wheel beside the one cherub** as a common expression of the culture to mean “there was one wheel beside each cherub.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with one wheel beside each cherub]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a stone of topaz** sparkles and gleams, so did **the wheels**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [was bright and sparkling, like the gleam of a topaz stone]
See how you translated the same word in 1:16.

10.note: See how you translated this same phrase in Ezekiel 1:16. Alternate translation: [it was just like two wheels at right angles, one inside the other]

11.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Here it introduces the reason why the wheels did not turn when they went. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

The implication is that **the head** refers to the head of each cherub, that is, the direction in which the cherub was facing. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the head of each cherub]

12.note: Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [for the four of them, that is, the wheels of all four of them were full of eyes]

13.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the wheels** with the information about what someone called them, rather than mentioning the wheels first and then referring to them again with the word **them**. Alternate translation: [The wheels were called]

The expression **was called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Ezekiel does not say who called the wheels by this name, so if you use an active form, you could use a general subject such as “someone.” Alternate translation: [someone called them]
Here, **in my ears** represents “as I listened.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [as I listened]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:6.

14.note: Ezekiel is using the possessive form to describe the four **faces** that each cherub had. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And each cherub had four faces]

15.note: The pronoun **It** refers to **the cherubs**, considered together as a group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The cherubs were the beings]
See how you translated this name in [1:1](ta:01).

16.note: The pronoun **they** in the phrase **also they** refers to **the wheels**, while the pronoun **them** in the phrase **from beside them** refers to the cherubs. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the wheels also stayed beside the cherubs]

17.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Here it introduces the reason why the wheels stood still and rose up along with the cherubs. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

18.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:28.
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:3.

19.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 10:2.

The pronoun **it** refers to **the glory of the God of Israel**, along with the cherubs that were carrying it. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the glory of God along with the cherubs stood]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:4.

20.note: Ezekiel is providing background information to help readers understand what is happening in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:15.
See how you translated this name in [1:1](ta:01).

21.note: Ezekiel is repeating the number **Four** in order to show that each cherub had four faces. If your language can repeat words to express this idea, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing this idea. Alternate translation: [A set of four faces]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:14.
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:8.

22.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the likeness of their faces** with the information about **the faces that I saw along the river of Kebar**, rather than mentioning the likeness of their faces first and then referring to it again with the word **they**. Alternate translation: [And the likeness of their faces was like the faces]

Here, **his faces** represents “the direction in which he was facing,” that is, straight ahead. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [straight ahead]
See how you translated this name in [1:1](ta:01).
